answers.reasoning: Ansor §5: task scheduler allocates tuning budget non-uniformly across subgraphs, prioritizing those with the largest marginal end-to-end gain (A). Motivation is that uniform budget wastes effort on already-optimal / low-contribution tasks (B). C confuses tuning budget with runtime dispatch. D fabricates a 10% floor rule.

A: FlashAttention's speedup is largest in the memory-bound long-sequence regime; short sequences may be compute-bound so speedup is smaller — correct per §5. C: block-wise tiling + online softmax, HBM traffic Θ(N²d/M) — correct core mechanism. D: FlashAttention v1 is exact (up to floating-point re-ordering). B is FALSE — v1 does NOT store the N×N attention matrix; the backward recomputes softmax from stored logsumexp + tiling. B is a very common misconception, so the paper explicitly refutes it.

B: peak > geomean; summarizing a paper by peak overstates typical benefit — correct scope discipline. C: paper numbers are conditioned on (workload, HW, baseline, stack); generalization requires additional evidence — correct. A wrongly ignores baseline dependence. D falsely equates peak with geomean.

Halide's separation of algorithm and schedule allows the same portable algorithm to be re-scheduled (tiled/vectorized/parallelized/fused/recomputed) per target without changing semantics. A/B/D mischaracterize the paper's argument.

MLIR's core design intent: express each optimization at its natural abstraction level with progressive lowering across dialects, sharing compiler infrastructure. A (single-IR) directly contradicts the paper. B (runtime dispatcher) is wrong. D (replace LLVM) is wrong — MLIR lowers to LLVM.

Kernel-level 3× ≠ end-to-end 3×. Amdahl's law bounds end-to-end speedup by fraction of runtime in the accelerated kernel; graph breaks, host overhead, and non-compiled subgraphs further cap it. A/B/D are technically wrong claims.

A: an ablation isolates a mechanism but does not establish head-to-head superiority — correct. C: quantization results are conditioned on model family/size/task/calibration — correct. D: wall-clock speedup depends on availability of an efficient dequant-GEMM kernel for the precision × granularity on the target GPU — correct. B is a canonical overclaim (universal ≥3× e2e speedup is unsupported).

Triton's tile-level abstraction: programmers write kernels over blocks of elements; the compiler handles per-thread PTX with coalescing, shared-memory staging, register tiling. A (targets CPU/TPU-only) is false. B (CUDA superset) is false. C (dispatcher) is false.

TVM argues that closed-form analytical models fail to reliably rank fine-grained schedule variants on modern hardware due to hard-to-model factors (cache, coalescing, register pressure, back-end choices), motivating a measurement-driven learned cost model. A/C/D misrepresent the paper.

PagedAttention targets KV-cache memory inefficiency from internal fragmentation (worst-case reservation waste) + external fragmentation (holes between sequences); fixed-size paged blocks with a page table enable more concurrent sequences. B/C/D describe schemes that are not PagedAttention.
